guide.metaDesc: Learn how to enjoy picture scrolls with horizontal scrolling: choosing a scroll, navigation, viewer features, and sharing.

scroll.title: Scroll horizontally
scroll.step1: Choose a scroll from the home page or the gallery. New visitors may start with Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga (Scroll A).
scroll.step2: Move through the scroll by swiping left/right, arrow keys, mouse wheel, or the horizontal scrollbar — as if unrolling a handscroll.
scroll.step3: Each scroll is divided into sections (scenes). Use the table of contents, #number URLs, or Next/Previous to follow the story.

features.tips: Viewing tips — pause at each section to take in the art. For Nine Stages of Decay scrolls, slow contemplative viewing is recommended.

faq.q: How do I navigate a picture scroll?
faq.a: Scroll horizontally. On phones, swipe; on desktop, use the mouse wheel, arrow keys, or horizontal scrollbar.

faq.q: Why horizontal scroll for vertical writing?
faq.a: Handscrolls were traditionally unrolled and viewed section by section. This site recreates that experience with horizontal scrolling.

faq.q: Can I jump to a specific scene?
faq.a: Yes — use #number in the URL, the table of contents, or Next/Previous buttons to move by section.

faq.q: How do I show captions or modern translation?
faq.a: Use the viewer buttons to toggle classical captions (kotoba-gaki) or modern Japanese/English translation.

kusouzuHub.metaDesc: Explore the stages of kusōzu (Nine Stages of Decay) and browse picture scrolls that depict each stage, viewable through horizontal scrolling on emakimono.com.
kusouzuHub.intro: Kusōzu (Nine Stages of Decay) is Buddhist art depicting nine stages of a corpse plus the living form — ten scenes from life to ashes. These works contrast beauty with impermanence and support meditative contemplation. On this site you can unroll kusōzu picture scrolls horizontally, scene by scene.
kusouzuHub.tips: Viewing tips — pause at each section to take in the art. For kusōzu scrolls, slow contemplative viewing is recommended.

choujuGigaHub.metaDesc: Browse all four scrolls of Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga (Frolicking Animals and Humans), Japan's oldest cartoon-like picture scrolls from the Heian-Kamakura period.
choujuGigaHub.metaDescEn: Browse all four scrolls of Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga (Frolicking Animals and Humans), Japan's oldest cartoon-like picture scrolls from the Heian-Kamakura period.
choujuGigaHub.intro: Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga (Frolicking Animals and Humans) is a set of four picture scrolls from the Heian-Kamakura period. Famous for humorous depictions of rabbits, monkeys, and frogs behaving like humans, it is often called Japan's oldest manga. Browse all four scrolls horizontally.

copyright.metaDesc: How copyright, public domain, and CC licenses apply to emaki images, plus guidelines for using them with AI image generators such as Stable Diffusion and Midjourney.
copyright.sectionTitle: Copyright & Licenses — AI Image Generation Guidelines
copyright.intro: When using emaki images, many people wonder whether classical works are free to use, or how licenses differ between overseas and Japanese institutions. This page explains how copyright and licenses apply to emaki images and provides practical guidelines for safe reuse. This page is for information purposes only and is not legal advice.

copyright.title: Copyright — classical emaki are in the public domain
copyright.body: Most emaki on this site were created between the Heian and Edo periods, and their creators died centuries ago. In Japan, copyright generally expires 70 years after the author's death, so the original works of these scrolls are in the public domain.
points: However, the important point is that the work itself and the image are different things. The conditions for using a photographed or digitized image are governed by the license set by the institution that holds the original (museum, library, or digital archive).
In other words, "the work is public domain, therefore the image is free to use" is not necessarily true. Please check the license of the institution that is the source of the image.
This site displays the source and processing information (resolution adjustment, WebP conversion, etc.) on each scroll page. When using an image, follow that source information.

links.name: Agency for Cultural Affairs (Japan) — Copyright overview (Japanese)

cc.title: CC licenses (Creative Commons)
cc.body: Creative Commons (CC) licenses are built from combinations of four conditions. First learn the four building blocks, then use the table below to see whether a license fits what you want to do. Images published by overseas digital archives (such as the MET and Wellcome Collection) often use CC licenses.

conditions.label: Attribution
conditions.desc: OK to use if you give credit

conditions.label: NoDerivatives
conditions.desc: Modifying or remixing is not allowed

conditions.label: ShareAlike
conditions.desc: Modified works must be shared under the same license

cc.note: As a rule, credits should include the work name, author, holding institution, source URL, and license name (e.g. CC BY 4.0). Terms differ by license version, so always check the license notice on the relevant page before use.

ai.title: Guidelines for AI image generation
ai.body: Guidelines by category for derivative works with Stable Diffusion, ControlNet, Midjourney, and similar tools.
points: Public domain / CC0 images: AI training, generation, publication, and commercial use are all allowed. Listing the source work and institution in your notes is good practice for derivative-work culture.
CC BY images: Generation and commercial use are allowed, but the required credit (attribution) must be attached to the output.

Institution-terms images (e.g. ColBase): Always check the "commercial use / modification / redistribution" clauses. Some institutions explicitly prohibit AI training. Using images against the terms is not permitted even if the original work is public domain.
Do not redistribute the images themselves: Avoid redistributing or selling the photographs or their processed versions as training datasets, as this may violate the institutions' licenses.
Do not misrepresent: Do not present outputs as if they were the actual collection item (or an institution's creation).

Check the AI tool's own terms too: Tool terms change frequently (e.g. Midjourney's commercial-use conditions, Adobe Firefly's training-data policies). Always check the terms current at the time of use.
